author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Iqaluit observes Remembrance Day at cadet hall
content:
The cadet hall in Iqaluit was overflowing with about 300 people during the Royal Legion’s Remembrance Day ceremony Wednesday morning.




The annual event began around 11 a.m. in both English and Inuktitut.




“Canada as a nation owes an everlasting debt of gratitude to the men and women who have served and continue to serve their country, in times of war and peace,” said legion Branch 168 president John Graham,  the master of ceremonies.




The day began with a march that included police, veterans and community members. It began at the RCMP building on Sivumugiaq Street and ended at the hall.




RCMP chaplain Paul Hitz spoke about sharing gratitude for those who served.




“It is also a day to express our gratitude to those who serve today, the members of our Canadian Armed Forces, including our Canadian Rangers who stand guard over the ideals we as Canadians cherish,” he said. “Lest we forget.”




Hitz also acknowledged the youth who joined the ceremony and highlighted the significance of their presence.
















Remembrance Day wreaths were laid at the cadet hall in Iqaluit on Wednesday during the Royal Canadian Legion’s annual Remembrance Day ceremony. (Photo by Lilli Akpaleepaik)




“To the youth among us, many of whom cannot yet imagine the realities of war, this day matters too. May your hearts and minds be stirred by what we place before you today,” he said

author: David Venn
title: QIA considers ‘next steps’ after NIRB recommends hydro plant move forward without review
content:
The Qikiqtani Inuit Association is “considering its next steps” after the Nunavut Impact Review Board recommended that Iqaluit’s proposed hydro project move forward without a public review.




“Our priority remains ensuring that the development of new energy infrastructure advances alongside the protection of Inuit rights,” reads a statement from QIA spokesperson Markoosie Qaunirq, issued Tuesday.




The $500-million Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Hydro Project, currently in its preliminary design phase, is proposed by Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp., a subsidiary of Qikiqtaaluk Corp., which is the QIA’s development arm.




If approved, it will lead to the construction of a hydroelectric plant able to produce up to 30 megawatts on the Kuugaaluk River, about 60 kilometres northeast of the city. It will also include a 7,136-hectare reservoir and a 66-kilometre access road.




NNC president Harry Flaherty has said the plant could replace 15 million litres of diesel fuel imported every year to generate electricity.




In November 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney named it a “nation-building” project to fast-track approvals. That move meant construction could begin in 2028 — two years earlier than originally anticipated.

title: Award-winning Mary Paningajak sees art as a way to heal
content:
Mary Paningajak grew up surrounded by art in Ivujivik.




She watched her father, Tivi Paningajak, make prints and sculptures, and she remembers visiting his studio.




“One time, he let me make a screen print,” Paningajak said in an interview Tuesday at Kuuujjuaq’s adult education centre.




She was nine years old when she first started making art and spent years learning different tools and techniques.




Now 65, her artistic practice has earned her northern Quebec’s artist of the year award from Quebec’s Council of Arts and Letters, or the Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec. It’s a $15,000 prize that recognizes her contribution to Nunavik’s arts community.




The council’s director general Véronique Fontaine presented the award on Nov. 8, during the opening night of the Path to 100 festival in Kuujjuaq, which commemorates the anniversary of the signing of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement.




“I was so surprised to hear that I won because there are lots of artists in Canada and Quebec. I was thinking, how come they chose me?” Paningajak said in an interview.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Six hopefuls in running for Kitikmeot Inuit Association president
content:
Six candidates have put their name forward in the Kitikmeot Inuit Association’s presidential election.




The organization that manages lands in trust for Kitikmeot Inuit will elect its president, a vice-president and three regional board of directors on Dec. 14.




Two other Inuit organizations, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. and Qikiqtani Inuit Association, will also host their 

leadership elections

 the same day.




The KIA presidential nominees are Jeannie Ehaloak, Rosabelle Klengenberg and Lawrence Otokiak from Cambridge Bay; Simon Komangat and Raymond Quqshuun Sr. from Gjoa Haven; and David Audlatak Nivingalok from Kugluktuk, according to a news release from the organization.




Since late June, Nivingalok has served as acting president after KIA announced former president James Eetoolook had to take leave “for personal matters.”




James Aiyout, Abel Aqqaq, David Aqqaq, and Ashoona Iroqiut hope to be elected to the board to represent Taloyoak.




Kugluktuk and Kugaaruk have one person running for their community’s spot on the board of directors: Leah Kadlun put her name forward for the Kugluktuk seat, and Tars Angutingunirk put his name forward to represent Kugaaruk.
















The nomination period for KIA’s social and cultural vice-president position has been extended until Friday.




Successful candidates will hold onto their roles until 2030.

title: $575M commitment a ‘first step’ in Inuit Child First transition, minister says
content:
The $575-million, five-year commitment to the Inuit Child First Initiative in Budget 2026 is the “first step” in a broader transition, says Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty.




The program, rebranded as Pirutsiagutiit and developed with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami and the four Inuit treaty organizations, is expected to launch April 1, 2027. Delivery will be transferred from Indigenous Services Canada to the treaty organizations or their designates.




“I’m really proud of the work that was done by ITK and all of the partners in the space for Inuit Child First Initiative,” Gull-Masty said during a news conference at the Inuusirvik Community Wellness Hub in Iqaluit on Saturday.




“We’ve had a lot of feedback. They’ve given us a lot of data. They’ve given us a lot of information. That’s what helped us to be able to bring forth the funding commitment.”




Gull-Masty said further announcements are expected from Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand and Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty.




“This is the first step in what you are going to see. The next step that comes forward is built with the essential input of our partners,” she said. 




ITK said in an email to Nunatsiaq News that it would provide more details in the coming weeks, as well.

title: Offshore Western Arctic oil and gas exploration could be back on the table
content:
The days might be numbered for the federal government’s decade-long 

moratorium

 on oil and gas exploration in the Western Arctic — at least in its present form.




“There is a review happening,” said Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand during a news conference at Nunavut Arctic College in Iqaluit on Tuesday.




The moratorium, established in December 2016 by then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, remains in place as the Liberal government charts “the best path forward,” Chartrand said.




The moratorium agreement calls for a review every five years. 

This includes ongoing meetings with Inuit organizations and territorial governments, Chartrand said.




At a news conference in Montreal at the same time, Prime Minister Mark Carney highlighted $11 million in funding to support “the governance and oversight of offshore oil and gas activities in the Arctic Ocean.”




“This is capacity funding for Inuit leadership. It is absolutely not in any way, shape, or form a decision about lifting the moratorium,” Carney said.

title: Kuujjuaq festival organizer hopes to spark conversation about Inuit identity
content:
For organizer Saali Kuata, the Path to 100 Festival offers an opportunity to move beyond commemorating the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement. It allows for Inuit to examine how it has shaped their communities.




Art can start that conversation.




“Art is just another language that we can use that can transcend language,” said Kuata, Avataq Cultural Institute program director, in an interview.




The Path to 100 festival celebrates the 50th anniversary of the JBNQA and takes place at the Katittavik Theatre in Kuujjuaq from Sunday to Wednesday. It features an art exhibition, performances and workshops, as well as discussions about cultural identity, futurism and economic development.




The governments of Quebec and Canada, as well as representatives for Nunavik Inuit and Crees of Eeyou Istchee, signed the the JBNQA on Nov. 11, 1975. It led to 

the creation

 of a school board, a regional government and health-care system in Nunavik.




The festival’s name, Path to 100, reflects a long-term vision for Inuit.




That means Inuit having greater control over the decisions that affect their communities while protecting their cultural identity and rights.

author: David Venn
title: Preparations for Nunavut devolution entering ‘final phase,’ premier’s office says
content:
Preparations for devolution are entering “their final phase,” Nunavut Premier John Main’s office said Tuesday in a news release.




The release provides an update on the Government of Nunavut’s devolution process, which will see control over a vast majority of Crown land in the territory 

transferred

 to the GN.




To enable devolution, Nunavut must 

mirror

 six pieces of federal legislation: The Waters Act, Public Lands Act, Archaeological and Palaeontological Sites Act, Surface Rights Tribunal Act, Nunavut Planning and Project Assessment Act, and the Canada Oil and Gas Operations Act.




MLAs passed four of those acts through second reading during the fall sitting of the legislative assembly. They include the Waters Act, the Surface Rights Tribunal Act, Public Lands Act and Archaeological and Palaeontological Sites Act.




The final two bills will be tabled during the winter sitting, said the release.




Work is also ongoing to create a new Department of Mines, Natural Resources and Land. The department has a new organizational structure and Inuktitut name: Nunalirijikkut.




“Many Nunavummiut who will work in the new department are currently employed by the [federal government],” the release said, adding that the deadline for such employees to respond to the GN’s job offer is Nov. 22.
















“Their knowledge and technical expertise are highly valued.”

author: Randi Beers
title: Expect office, road closures Wednesday for Remembrance Day
content:
Parts of downtown Iqaluit will be closed to traffic Wednesday morning to allow for a Remembrance Day ceremony and march to take place.




The closures will affect parts of Sivumugiaq Street and Mivvik Street starting at 9:30 a.m. until approximately 12 p.m., the City of Iqaluit announced Monday in a public service announcement.




“The closure is necessary to ensure the safety of participants and the public while the march is underway,” said the announcement.




The march, which starts at the RCMP detachment and ends at the cadet hall, is scheduled to start at 10:30 a.m.




Remembrance Day ceremonies are also planned in Rankin Inlet at the Singiituq Complex, from 10:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. and Cambridge Bay’s community hall at 10:30.




Government offices across the territory will also be closed to mark the day.




Remembrance Day is observed every year on Nov. 11 to honour armed forces members who have died in the line of duty.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit Northern store’s security guards get tactical makeover
content:
Iqaluit’s Northern store unveiled a 

new look

 in October, following three years of in-store renovations. Its security guards also got a makeover.




Some of their new all-black tactical uniforms come with accessories, including body-worn cameras and what appear to be retractable batons.




“Two guards per shift have cameras and they are only turned on during an event,” Brigitte Burgoyne, spokesperson for the North West Co., the Winnipeg-based parent corporation of Northern, said in an email.




“The North West Company does not collect body camera footage.”




Canadian Arctic Protective Services does, the company’s regional manager said.




That’s who North West Co. contracts for its security.




With a head office in Iqaluit, Canadian Arctic Protective Services provides security services across Nunavut, and in Ottawa and Yellowknife, “and soon in Miami, Florida,” its website says.
















“Footage access is limited to select management personnel and is used to review incidents and, where required, for law enforcement or legal proceedings,” said Paul Hunter, the security company’s regional director, in an email. 




“The cameras are turned on during an event and do not record continuously. They are not used for general customer surveillance.”




Hunter declined to say if the tool on the guard’s belt is a baton.




“We do not publicly share our internal security procedures or comment on site-specific security arrangements,” Hunter said.




Loblaws Inc., Canada’s largest food retailer, launched a pilot project using body cameras across B.C., Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario in early 2025. 

Shoppers Drug Mart followed.




“I take this as a completely misguided approach to the issue of food insecurity,” said sociologist Alissa Overend, interim director of the Research Institute of Urban Wellness at 

Edmonton’s MacEwan University, in a phone interview.
















“Even in cities, I don’t think policing is the right approach, but especially in northern and remote communities,” Overend said. “There have been criticisms of racial profiling.”




Shopper Marion Kusugak learned about some of the store’s on-site security arrangements first-hand on Thursday evening when a guard grabbed her backpack from her and then searched it, as she’d just begun shopping. 

(The guard who interacted with Kusugak is not the guard in the main photo of this story.)




Nunatsiaq watched as a 

guard dumped all her possessions on the checkout counter. 




“Be careful, please,” Kusugak said.




Some of her belongings fell to the floor as he rooted through them.
















Northern store shopper Marion Kusugak shows the red ticket a cashier gave her after her backpack was taken and searched by a security guard on Thursday evening. She was not wearing sunglasses and a hood when the guard stopped her. She wore them only for the photo. (Photo by Daron Letts)




When the search was over, the guard stuffed her things back in her backpack. Then the cashier took the bag and put it out of sight behind the counter and handed Kusugak a red ticket.




“It’s a new policy,” the cashier told her.




After a pause, Kusugak asked the guard his first name, then put her hand out to shake his. He didn’t shake her hand.




Asked how she felt about the search as she pushed her cart down the frozen food aisle, she said, “I didn’t like it.”




“This was a town first and then it became a city,” she said.




Burgoyne at North West Co., and Hunter at Canadian Arctic Protective Services declined requests to answer questions about whether the way the guard searched Kusugak’s backpack was standard practice or whether it was appropriate.




Down the street at Arctic Ventures, elder Seemeega Kootoo staffs the entrance six days a week. He is one of three local security guards at the store.




Iqaluit elder Seemeega Kootoo staffs the door at Arctic Ventures in Iqaluit on Wednesday evening. He is one of three local security guards at the store. (Photo by Daron Letts)




“When people who are barred from here come, I don’t let them in,” he said during an interview on Wednesday. “That’s what I do.”

When he is not busy, he returns shopping carts to their stall, he added.




Arctic Co-op stores use fixed in-store surveillance systems to address theft concerns “in the least invasive manner,” said company vice-president Duane Wilson. The company has also not adopted body-worn cameras for security staff because they require detailed policies around when to record, as well as accessing, storing and retaining footage.




Iqaluit RCMP have responded to an average of fewer than 10 shoplifting-related calls per month between January and October, said spokesperson Sgt. George Henrie.




On the North West Co. website, it states:




“In the spirit of Truth and Reconciliation, we acknowledge Canada’s colonial history and the policies of racism that created power imbalances throughout history and the resulting harm done to Indigenous Peoples,” under the heading: “Our promise to Indigenous Peoples.”

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: John Amagoalik seeks funding to stay in Nunavut while case winds through court
content:
Lawyers for John Amagoalik are scheduled to appear in court Friday in the hope of securing emergency funding that would allow him to stay in his home while his lawsuit against the Nunavut government proceeds.




Last month, the retired politician filed an 

application for a judicial review

 in response to the Department of Health’s refusal to fund his medical care and housing in Iqaluit.




Amagoalik is revered by many as the “Father of Nunavut.” He dedicated decades of his life to advancing Inuit rights.




He had been living at the Embassy West long-term care home in Ottawa before returning to Iqaluit this summer. While his goal is to 

live his final days

 in the territory he helped create, his family says they can’t afford to make that happen without funding from Nunavut’s Health Department.




The department has stated this type of funding 

does not fall

 under its authority.




Nunavut Chief Justice Susan Cooper is scheduled to preside over Friday’s hearing, said Andrew Morrison, among the lawyers that represent Amagoalik. She’s set to decide whether to grant funding that would allow Amagoalik to remain in Nunavut during the judicial review process.

title: Rankin Inlet taxi service shuts down after nearly 6 years
content:
After nearly six years of driving residents around Rankin Inlet, Silu’s Taxi has closed.




Owner Silu Autut announced the closure Nov. 5 on Facebook, saying the cost of keeping vehicles on the road had become too much to justify continuing the service.




“The breakdowns and the cost of maintenance kept adding up, especially with what the cost of living is nowadays, and the long hours do catch up at the end,” Autut said to Nunatsiaq News in an interview conducted over Facebook Messenger.




Silu’s Taxi opened in February 2021, after the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.




“I started it for the town, to make sure the town is taken care of, not just to make money,” Autut said. 




The taxi operated daily, starting at 8 a.m. and usually running until at least 10 p.m. 




On Fridays and Saturdays, service often continued until midnight.
















“Sometimes, in the cold winter months or in the rain, we would pick up people walking by with an amauti carrying their infants, just to get them out of the cold and home safe,” Autut said.

title: Four candidates step up in NTI leadership election
content:
Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. has announced who will be running in its Dec. 14 election, where two vice-presidential roles are up for grabs.




Paul Irngaut, NTI’s vice-president since 2022, is seeking re-election.




Robert Bourassa, Adamee Itorcheak and Aaron Aopaloktok Pedersen are also vying for a leadership role.




NTI currently only has one vice-president position. The second vice-president position is new.




Annie Thomlinson, an NTI spokesperson, said the organization added another vice-president position in response to the “growing workload and operational requirements of NTI.”




The two vice-presidents will be assigned duties with consideration given to their strength and interests, said an information sheet provided to Nunatsiaq News about the roles.




For example, the successful candidates may be assigned to chair any of the NTI board committees, including finance, wildlife and environment, social and cultural development, infrastructure and housing, or lands.
















Vouchers will again be offered to those who show up at polls on election day, Thomlinson said.




In May, the organization 

offered

 $100 grocery vouchers to beneficiaries who showed up to its by-election. Thomlinson said more details should be released shortly.

ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᖅ ᒪᑐᐃᓚᐅᙱᓐᓂᖓᓂ ᕿᓚᒻᒥᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖃᙱᑦᑐᒃᑯᕕᐅᓂᖓᓂ, ᓯᒥᒃᑕᐅᑎᑦ ᐅᖅᑰᓴᐅᑎᖓᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᖓᓂ ᐃᓇᖏᖅᑕᐅᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ, ᓄᓇᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᕐᓇᙱᑦᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓄᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᖅᑎᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᖃᕋᓴᐅᔭᑎᒍᑦ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐋᔩᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᔨ ᔭᓐᑐᓪ ᐱᓕᐊᑦ−ᔫᓯᐱ ᓇᒃᓯᐅᔾᔭᖓᓂ ᓄᓇᑦᓯᐊᖅ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 27−ᒥ.




ᑕᐃᒪᐃᑦᑕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ, ᐅᖅᑰᓴᐅᑎᖓᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᒥ ᖃᒥᑎᑕᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᓪᓗᓄᑦ ᑕᓪᓕᒪᓄᑦ.




ᐊᐃᑉᕆᓕᒥ, ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᕐᓇᙱᑦᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᖏᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖓᕙ ᑐᓚᑦᑕᕐᕕᒃ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᕕᖓ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᐊᑲᐅᙱᓕᐅᕈᑕᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᑉ ᐅᖅᑰᓴᐅᑎᖓᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᓯᖏᓐᓂ “ᐊᖏᔪᓂ ᐱᔭᕆᑐᔪᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓂ.” ᑕᐃᒪᐃᓐᓂᖓᓄᑦ, ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᑦ ᓅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᓂ ᒪᓐᑐᕆᐋᓪᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒪᑐᓯᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᐅᔪᒥ.




ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 23−ᒥ, ᑰᔾᔪᐊᖅ ᒪᐃᔭᐅᑉ ᑐᒡᓕᖓ ᑯᓘᑦ ᒑᑦᐳᐊᐃ ᐅᖃᐅᔾᔨᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᕼᐋᒻᓚᒃᑯᓐᓂ, ᐃᒡᓗᓕᕆᔨᕐᔪᐊᒃᑯᓐᓂ, ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᕐᓇᙱᑦᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᖏᓐᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᕕᖓ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᖅᑎᑦᑎᕗᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᒥ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᖃᙱᑦᑐᒃᑯᕕᐅᓂᖓᓂ ᑎᑭᓐᓇᓱᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 2027−ᒧᑦ.

title: Police seize liquor, cash in Nunavik-Quebec investigation
content:
A man from Chambly, Que., and a woman from Kangiqsujuaq could face charges following a police investigation into the illegal possession and sale of alcohol.




The Sûreté du Québec’s Contraband Investigation Unit, working with the Nunavik Police Service, searched a property in Kangiqsujuaq on Wednesday. 




The investigation, which began in June, also led to a search in Chambly on Tuesday, after investigators determined the two cases were linked.




The searches resulted in the seizure of nearly eight litres of various alcoholic beverages and close to $12,000 in Canadian currency, according to a news release issued Thursday by the Quebec provincial police.




The individuals involved are a 34-year-old man from Chambly and a 32-year-old woman from Kangiqsujuaq. The news release did not provide their names. They could face charges related to illegal possession of alcohol and selling it without the required permits under Quebec’s Act respecting offences relating to alcoholic beverages.

title: Ottawa’s International Inuit Day brings communities together
content:
Clyde River seamstress Sarah Kiliktee had never seen a traditional sealskin tent before she helped build one in Ottawa.




Kiliktee travelled south to teach members of Ottawa-based Isaruit Inuit Arts how to construct an ittaq, a traditional Inuit tent made from sealskins.




Pangnirtung singer-songwriter Joey Nowyuk performs in Inuktitut for a crowd at Isaruit Inuit Arts’ sixth annual International Inuit Day celebration at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa on Saturday. (Photo by Nehaa Bimal)




The project began Oct. 26 and was completed 10 days later, just in time for Saturday’s International Inuit Day celebration at Annie Pootoogook Park in Ottawa’s Sandy Hill neighbourhood, near the University of Ottawa.







Twenty-five sealskins were stitched together to make the tent that was on display at the park for visitors to step inside.




Kiliktee said the group of nine seamstresses relied on Google Images for reference because sealskin tents are no longer commonly used. They repeatedly checked measurements and patched holes around the flippers and tails of the skins.




“This is our first time and it turned out good, so we’re happy with it,” she said.
















Kiliktee said she came to Ottawa specifically for the celebration and was scheduled to leave early Sunday morning.

title: Six months to fix foster care failures is a tall order
content:
Six months isn’t much time to fix a problem that has festered for 15 years.




But that’s the task ahead for the Government of Nunavut after the federal auditor general presented a scathing report on the state of foster care in Nunavut, pointing to “fundamental weaknesses” that have persisted for years.




Deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes presented the report titled 

Foster Care in Nunavut

 on Tuesday. It’s the fifth time the office of the auditor general — responsible for probing the effectiveness of government programs — has looked into Nunavut’s foster care since 2011.




The Family Services Department can remove children from their family homes and place them in foster care when their parents aren’t able to meet their needs or provide a safe environment.

author: Randi Beers
title: Jimmy Bell – The ghost of Arctic Bay
content:
At Cape Dorset in 1949, Jimmy Bell, the large, fun-loving Hudson’s Bay Co. trader, took ill. His once rotund body began to waste away until he was but a shadow of his former self. 




On arriving in Cape Dorset, his young clerk, Peter Murdoch, who had known Jimmy in Lake Harbour, barely recognized him. He described him as “a skinny-looking fellow wearing baggy clothes, his face lined and his eyes a sickly yellow.”  




Officials in Winnipeg knew in February that Jimmy’s health was “not up to its usual robust standard,” but Jimmy attributed it to “too much of his own cooking.” 




In May he sent a message to Winnipeg that admitted he required medical attention. Another message followed, in which he said he would go out to Churchill on the supply ship for a check-up. But he kept the extent of his illness from his superiors. He surmised, correctly, that if they knew his true condition, they would evacuate him to the south. 




But Peter Murdoch knew that Jimmy needed attention, much more than he could provide using the post’s medical manual. He thought that Jimmy had stomach cancer. Without Jimmy’s knowledge, Murdoch sent a telegram by radio to Winnipeg informing them of Jimmy’s condition. Too late, Jimmy realized what Murdoch had done and mustered all his strength to roar at Murdoch and express his disapproval. 




Jimmy told Murdoch, “If I have cancer I want to die in the North. I want my spirit to stay in the North. When I die my spirit is going back to Arctic Bay. That’s the place I really love most – Arctic Bay.” 




But Winnipeg had got the message. Headquarters immediately dispatched their Canso aircraft, nicknamed Polar Bear, on the long flight to Cape Dorset.
















Jimmy was evacuated to Winnipeg on July 2. He was operated on at Winnipeg General Hospital a few days later, but doctors concluded that there was nothing more they could do for him. His mother and a brother were sent for and reached his bedside on the last day of August. Jimmy Bell died on Sept. 12 and was buried in Brookside Cemetery, in Winnipeg. He was only 43.




The inscription on his pink granite headstone ends with: “Here we leave our loved one sleeping.” 




But Jimmy wasn’t sleeping. He was restless. And, as he had promised, his spirit returned to Arctic Bay — or so it appeared.




Jimmy had a dear friend there. Amarualik was a leader among the Inuit and had worked for the Hudson’s Bay Co. for many years. Jimmy and Amarualik were close, and Jimmy had had a child with Amarualik’s daughter, Kautaq. That girl, Tapisa (now Tapisa Hughes of Arctic Bay) was the youngest of three daughters that Jimmy had with Inuit women.




When he died, the Hudson’s Bay Co. manager’s residence in Arctic Bay became the scene of strange occurrences. Residents and visitors heard footsteps in the storeroom, but there was no one there. Cups rattled in the cupboards and dishes rattled in the sink. But no one present had disturbed them. Doors mysteriously opened. The building was haunted.




Jimmy had returned to Arctic Bay to be near his old friend, Amarualik.
















It’s noteworthy that many of Jimmy’s manifestations happened in the kitchen of the residence, because Jimmy, in life, had apparently been obsessed with the neatness of his kitchen. Len Budgell, a lifelong Hudson’s Bay Co. employee, recalled that Jimmy was a bachelor and that “he liked things just so. If you did the dishes at night and hung the tea towel up, and it wasn’t the way Jimmy would have hung it up, in the morning you would find it neatly rearranged to Jimmy’s preference.” 




When the rattling of dishes became too loud, some company managers were known to shout, “Leave the bloody dishes alone, Jimmy.” 




That would generally result in a short burst of fierce rattling — Jimmy was clearly displeased — before silence would settle in. 




Soon after Eric Mitchell arrived in Arctic Bay as manager, he experienced a number of “curious, though disturbing incidents.” Footsteps were heard on the creaky floorboards of the attic night after night until one night he shouted, “Quit it!” 




One night he awoke to find all the doors of the house wide open. When he told Amarualik about these events, the old Inuk replied nonchalantly, “That’s just Jimmy Bell wandering around. Don’t worry about it; he’s just waiting for me to join him.” 
















The disturbances in Arctic Bay were no secret. They became part of Baffin Island lore. Word of the haunted staff house reached Winnipeg where some officials laughed it off. 




But one winter in the 1960s, company officials visited Arctic Bay and overnighted at the staff house. They wanted to investigate the reports of Jimmy’s ghost. Footsteps were said to have been heard on the roof, and so, on a windless night, they put a ladder up and spread flour on the roof, then waited. Sure enough, footsteps were heard again on the roof. But a physical check showed the flour undisturbed.




Amarualik passed away on June 28, 1967. The disturbances ceased at that time. Jimmy Bell’s friend had finally joined him, and Jimmy was finally at peace. 




Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. Kenn Harper is a historian and writer who lived in the Arctic for over 50 years. He is the author of 

Give Me Winter, Give Me Dogs: Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition

, and 

Thou Shalt Do No Murder

, among other books. Feedback? Send your comments and questions to kennharper@hotmail.com.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: International Inuit Day celebration set to return to Ottawa’s Annie Pootoogook Park
content:
Isaruit Inuit Arts, an Ottawa-based organization, will host its sixth annual International Inuit Day celebration Saturday at Annie Pootoogook Park in the Sandy Hill neighbourhood. 




The event runs from noon to 4:30 p.m. and will feature musical performances, a feast, family games and cultural activities. It is free and open to the public. 




Performers include Pangnirtung singer-songwriter Joey Nowyuk, Ottawa-based drum dancer Donovan Gordon Tootoo, who is originally from Rankin Inlet, and the Nunavut Sivuniksavut students’ performing group.




Inuit arts and crafts vendors will also sell their work at the event.




The schedule includes a qulliq lighting at 1:30 p.m., performances from 1:40 p.m., a feast at 2:30 p.m. and community games at 3:15 p.m. 




An Inuit cultural activity tent will offer a qulliq making activity and photo opportunities featuring Inuit clothing.




International Inuit Day, observed annually on Nov. 7, was established by the Inuit Circumpolar Council in 2006 to celebrate Inuit culture and amplify Inuit voices across the circumpolar world.
















The date honours Greenlander Eben Hopson Sr., founder of the first Inuit Circumpolar Conference in 1977.

author: Daron Letts
title: MLAs wrap up fall sitting
content:
The fall sitting of Nunavut’s legislative Assembly wrapped up Thursday, with MLAs passing into law seven bills they introduced, leaving four to be dealt with later. 




“Thank you, each and every one of you, for working hard for the two weeks of what we did,” said Speaker David Joanasie, the MLA for South Baffin, as he closed the session at the end of the day.




MLAs looked at 11 bills over the two weeks that that they sat, beginning on Oct. 22, including legislation to increase the student loan limit, changes to the membership of the board of inquiry that governs medical professionals, and an approval for capital expenditures.




Among the bills that were passed were:







Bill 15: an act to amend the Student Financial Assistant Act to double the limit of loans made to a person who is eligible to receive other loans to $300,000.




Bill 14: an amendment to the Medical Profession Act to update the membership composition of the Board of Inquiry, set out term limits for members of the Board of Inquiry, establish hearing panels, and modernize the law’s language. 




Bill 10: Appropriation (Capital) Act, a bill that authorizes capital expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2028.







The policymakers are scheduled to return to the Legislative Assembly in the new year on Feb. 27.

title: Clyde River grieves hamlet councillor, victim of Iqaluit homicide
content:

Steven Aipellee, her brother, said she had been visiting Iqaluit with her partner when when she was fatally stabbed on Oct. 17.




“It’s unbelievable, that happening to the family,” he said in a phone interview from Clyde River on Friday. She had one sister and five brothers.




Nunavut RCMP had reported her death to the public on Oct. 19, but didn’t identify her then. Police 

charged

title: Ottawa renews Inuit Child First Initiative funding, tops up Nutrition North
content:
The federal government is committing $575 million over five years to Inuit children’s services and more than $610 million over four years to northern food subsidies in this year’s federal budget.




The Liberal government released its budget for 2026-27, titled “Masters of our Destiny,” on Thursday.




It proposes renewing the Inuit Child First Initiative and transitioning it to Pirutsiagutiit, an Inuit-designed program developed with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami and the four Inuit treaty organizations.




The $575-million commitment would begin in the 2027-28 fiscal year. Pirutsiagutiit is expected to begin April 1, 2027, and will be operated by the treaty organizations or their designates, according to ITK.




Launched in September 2018, the Inuit Child First Initiative provides health, social, educational and other support to Inuit children and youth. Funding for the program ran out in 2025 and it 

has received

 one-year top ups since then, with the 

promise to retool

 it.




ITK had requested $600 million over five years for Pirutsiagutiit in its pre-budget submission. 




The budget also proposes $610.3 million over four years, beginning in 2027-28, for Nutrition North Canada and associated initiatives. It includes another $118.1 million in 2031-32, followed by $117 million annually.

author: Daron Letts
title: Experts decry Nunavut’s ‘Band-Aid’ approach to foster care
content:
The broken child welfare system in Nunavut is rooted in the territorial government’s colonial approach to the problem, say some with years of experience with the system.




“The taking of Indigenous children never stopped at residential school,” said Jeremy Young, who was separated from his mother as a child. “It only continued with foster care.”




Young spoke to Nunatsiaq News about his experience in Nunavut’s foster care system Thursday in response to the latest 

report

 by the federal auditor general

 i

nto the territorial government’s handling of youth in its care.




Tuesday’s report, the fifth over 15 years, shows little has changed. The Nunavut government is failing to account for the number of children in its care, failing to do consistent check-ins and failing in its duty to make sure every foster child is put into an appropriate home.




Young, now 26 years old, was taken from his mother as a child in Pangnirtung even though she did her best, Young said.




He blamed overcrowding and poverty for his family’s situation, saying his mother tried for 12 years to get housing for her family but ultimately could not.




“Society has failed Indigenous people,” he said. “That’s why we live in poverty. That’s why we go through the traumas we went through.”
















Young believes Inuit self-government is the antidote to the problems in the foster care system.

“ᐅᑯᐊ ᐊᖏᔪᑦ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᕐᕖᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᑐᓂᓯᕙᙱᑦᑎᐊᕐᑐᑦ. ᐊᑭᓕᕐᓱᐃᕙᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᑭᓕᐅᑎᓂᒃ ᑖᒃᓰᔭᕈᑎᓂᒃ. ᐊᑭᓕᕐᓱᐃᕙᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒋᔭᐅᔪᒥᒃ. ᐃᓄᖕᓂᓪᓗ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᑦᑎᕙᙱᖢᑎᒃ. ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᑎᒍᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖃᑦᑕᙱᑦᑐᑦ ᐅᕙᑦᑎᑐᑦ.”




ᑲᓇᑎ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᐅᔨᓕᓚᐅᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᑭᒋᑎᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᓄᕐᓯᕚ9ᓕᕐᓂᐊᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᖅᑕᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᓇᒻᒪᒃᓴᙱᑦᑐᖃᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᒫᓂ $120-ᓂ ᐊᑭᑦᑐᕆᐊᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᖃᑦᑕᐅᔭᕆᔭᐅᕙᒃᑐᑦ ᓂᐅᕕᕐᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᕘᓇ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᕕᐊᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᕗᐊᐃᓂᒥ ᓂᐅᕕᕐᕕᖕᓂ ᔪᓚᐃ ᐃᓱᓕᓕᕐᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᑲᓇᑎ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᐅᖃᖃᑎᖃᓕᕋᒥ ᐊᐅᔭᖅ ᐃᓱᓕᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᑭᐅᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐅᕆᔭᐅᓇᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᕐᒥᒃ ᕕᐊᓕᐅᖅᑕᖏᑦᑕ ᓴᙱᓂᖏᑦ ᒥᒃᖠᒋᐊᖅᑕᐅᓗᐊᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ.

title: Nunavut’s addictions treatment centre to open its doors for tour next week
content:
Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre will open its doors to the public for the first time next week in an open house.




Health Minister Janet Pitsiulaaq Brewster announced the event in a minister’s statement in the legislative assembly Wednesday.




She announced the open house, hosted by the territorial government, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., and Indigenous Services Canada, will take place on Nov. 13, but did not announce a time.




“This will be an opportunity for Nunavummiut to tour Aqqusariaq and recognize the people and partnerships behind it,” Brewster said.




The $87-million Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre is located across from the Arctic Winter Games Arena in Iqaluit.




Planning for the facility has been 

underway

 for more than a decade, Brewster said during her statement, and while “substantial completion” of the building is done, more work is needed before the facility can begin taking in patients.




The official opening date has yet to be announced, and the Inuit-led not-for-profit 

tasked with operating

 the facility will announce it when Aqqusariaq is ready for intake to begin, said Brewster.

A Canadian Coast Guard helicopter and a Royal Canadian Air Force Hercules aircraft assisted. Community members organized ground searches, including trips to Peel Inlet, on the northern coast of King William Island.
















The neighbouring community of

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Quebec coroner looking into death of Inuk girl
content:
A Quebec coroner is investigating the death of a four-year-old Inuk girl who died while under the supervision of Montreal’s youth protection services.




The girl, whose mother is from Nunavik, died in a hospital on March 31, after a worker at Batshaw Youth and Family Centres failed to respond to a request for an urgent visit at her family home, according to reporting by 

Radio-Canada.




“We can confirm that an investigation into the causes and circumstances of this death is being conducted,” said Jake Lamotta Granato, a spokesperson for Quebec’s coroner’s office, in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




Coroner Steeve Poisson has been assigned to the case, Lamotta Granato said.




“At the end of his investigation, should he deem it appropriate, the coroner may also issue recommendations aimed at protecting human life and preventing deaths under similar circumstances,” he said.




In late July, Santé Québec, which oversees health and social services in the province, announced it had ordered its inspection office to investigate the quality of youth protection services offered under its agency for Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal — Universitaire area, which has jurisdiction over Batshaw.




The announcement about the investigation came days after the Montreal Gazette revealed three youth under Batshaw’s care — including the four year old girl — had 

died suddenly in March

.

title: GN plans new bidding process to run Ottawa medical boarding home
content:
The Government of Nunavut plans to issue a new request for proposals for the operation of Larga Baffin, a boarding home for Inuit travelling to Ottawa for medical reasons.




The move is the latest in protracted negotiations between Larga Baffin Ltd., the facility’s current operator, and the territorial government, and could affect 

expansion plans

 for the facility.




Larga Baffin submitted a response to the GN’s initial request for proposals, which closed in May 2024, to operate the boarding home, but no contract was awarded, company president Malaya Zehr said in an Oct. 29 email to Nunatsiaq News.




The proposed contract was to run for 20 years, with two optional five-year renewal periods, for a potential total of 30 years.




The long-term agreement was intended to help a succe1ssful bidder secure financing to obtain or build a facility that met the capacity requirements, said former Nunavut health minister John Main two years ago in the legislative assembly.




For years Larga Baffin has been 

working through

 Ottawa’s municipal planning process to build a 

six-storey, 220-room facility at Hunt Club Road and Sieveright Avenue — about five kilometres northeast of the the Ottawa airport — that would accommodate up to 350 guests.




The existing facility on Richmond Road can hold 195 guests.
















Larga Baffin bought the Hunt Club Road property in 2020.

title: Tuberculosis documentary shows healing through sharing stories
content:
Iqaluit’s Astro Theatre was filled with people Tuesday evening for the première of a documentary that follows a group of tuberculosis survivors and youth as they find closure over their forced relocations decades ago.




Between the 1940s-1960s, the federal government transported thousands of Inuit to southern sanatoriums for tuberculosis treatment without their consent or without informing them about what was happening.




Many Inuit never returned home.




Taqqut Productions joined hands with The SeeChange Initiative to create 

Our Elders are so Important to Us: A Tuberculosis Sanatorium Healing Journey

, a 29-minute documentary that follows youth and survivors as they connect over these relocations, in an effort to provide healing and closure.




“If we value our elders as much as we say we do as Inuit, why not listen to their stories,” asked Naomi Tatty, the intercultural health lead at SeeChange, a non-profit and one of the leads for the documentary.




“Why not put their words out there and help us younger generations, and the generations ahead of us, understand what our families went through?”

title: Nunavut to receive $65.3M in additional federal funding for housing
content:
Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. will receive $65.3 million in federal funding for Inuit housing over five years, an expenditure MP Lori Idlout says is welcome but must be part of a long-term commitment to address the territory’s housing crisis.




“I know that when I still go to the communities, housing is always the first thing that’s mentioned to me as an important issue,” Idlout said in an interview Wednesday. 

“It’s great to see our government hearing that.”




The funding comes from a $130.3-million top up to the federal government’s Urban, Rural and Northern Indigenous Housing Strategy, which Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty announced Oct. 30 in Kuujjuaq.




The money will go to the four Inuit Treaty Organizations, including $32.5 million to Makivvik, nearly $17 million to the Inuvialuit Regional Corp. and $15.5 million to the Nunatsiavut Government.

author: Daron Letts
title: Auditor general points out ‘fundamental weaknesses’ in Nunavut’s foster care
content:
This story was updated on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at 5:53 p.m. ET.




Nunavut’s Department of Family Services “did not provide timely and effective foster care services to protect and support the safety and well-being of children,” says Canada’s deputy auditor general Andrew Hayes.




Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok sits in the Legislative Assembly last week. On Tuesday, Canada’s auditor general published a report that found her department “did not provide timely and effective foster care services to protect and support the safety and well-being of children.” (File photo by Lilli Akpaleeapik)




He tabled the report, 

Foster Care in Nunavut

, in the legislative assembly Tuesday. Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok had announced in March that the audit was underway.




“Fundamental weaknesses” in the territory’s foster care system includes “failures to maintain regular contact with children in care, weaknesses in the screening and monitoring of foster homes, and unreliable information on children and their placements,” according to a news release issued by the auditor general’s office Tuesday, ahead of Hayes’ tabling of the report.




While it’s estimated that about 400 children are in the foster care system, the department remains unaware of the exact number or where the children are located, the latest report states.




This is despite the department rolling out a

 

centralized reporting framework

 called Matrix three years ago.
















The audit states that the department relied on a manually compiled list instead of using the software.




Additionally, the department failed to keep up monthly in-person contact with children and foster caregivers, “a basic safeguard intended to protect children in care,” the report states.




“In more than 90 per cent of the files we reviewed, there was no evidence that the required monthly contact with children or foster care caregivers had been maintained,” Hayes said at a press conference in the legislative assembly, where he tabled the report earlier in the afternoon.




In five cases, there was no documented contact with a child for more than one year, including one gap of more than 17 months.




The report also found cracks in the department’s screening process. Family services conducted 52 per cent of home studies, which evaluate the safety of a foster home, before it placed a child.




Long-term monitoring also fell short, with annual reviews that confirmed a foster home remained safe were missing or 

incomplete in 62 per cent of examined cases.
















Caregivers were not given important information about a child — such as health, family or trauma history — in 32 of 44 files.




An onboarding process for new caregivers was absent, training for caregivers was infrequent 

and the foster caregiver manual had not been updated in more than 10 years, the report states.




“There’s recruitment and retention issues that the department needs to address,” Hayes said. “In some cases, housing can be a problem.”




Previous audits in

 2011

,

 2014

,

 2023

 and

 2025

 found similar problems, including one finding from 2023 that the department

 could not provide

 an accurate count for the number of children in its care.




Following the October 2023 report, former family services minister Margaret Nakashuk 

apologized

 for the department’s failure to protect children in its care.
















“Ultimately, we need to see more from the department and improve services to these families and children,” Hayes said.




“Hopefully there is an urgency that is being recognized by the department and that the legislative assembly members can use our report and the department’s responses to hold the department accountable for making the improvements that they’ve committed to.”




The auditor general will release another report in the spring of 2027, on the department’s “quality assurance work,” he said.




Akearok thanked the auditor general for the report and its recommendations, saying it validates many of the actions already underway in her department.




“Meaningful change requires accountability, consistent follow-through, and sustained action,” she said in a Government of Nunavut news release issued after the report was tabled.




Akearok said her department is strengthening prevention and family supports, improving oversight, equipping staff with tools and training, and supporting foster caregivers.

title: Ikur’raq cabin program expands with $500,000 in federal money
content:
The federal government has topped up a cabin program meant to reduce homelessness in Nunavut, Family Services Minister Gwen Healey Akearok announced Oct. 27.




Close to $514,000 will go towards the territory’s Ikur’raq Cabins Initiative, a project meant to give people a temporary place of respite from overcrowding, violence and addiction issues. The money will fund 15 cabins.




“Out-of-shelter homelessness is a major public health and safety issue,” Akearok said in her minister’s statement at the legislative assembly. “The Ikur’raq cabins offer a practical response to this urgent need.”




The GN funded the 

first set of 16 cabins

 in 2022 and the program was revived in 2025 with $1 million in federal money to build 20 additional cabins.




Akearok’s Oct. 27 announcement will bring the total to 51.




Hamlets, non-profits and hunters and trappers organizations can apply for $50,000 grants with the new round of funding.

title: NTI has a plan to adapt to climate change but needs money to implement it
content:
Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. has set a new vision for responding to climate change in the territory.




The plan – Anijaarniq Strategy: An Inuit Approach to Addressing Climate Change in Nunavut – identifies 15 goals based on engagement sessions with Nunavummiut. 




Nunavut’s three Inuit associations, the Kitikmeot Inuit Association, Kivalliq Inuit Association, and Qikiqtani Inuit Association hosted the workshops over 2024 and 2025. 




“This is one of the most intensive processes I believe that we’ve gone through in terms of the development of a strategy,” 

 said NTI research director Cheryl Wray, who oversaw the development of the 

Anijaarniq Strategy

.




The plan calls on the territorial and federal governments to commit money to achieve the goals identified in it, which include building more climate-resilient housing; transitioning to renewable energy systems; and creating Inuit-led climate research and adaptation programs. 




“We require funding for this plan to be actionable,” Wray said. 

“This is a plan which requires all partners to come to the table.”




She said NTI has yet to decide how much to ask for from each government.

author: Randi Beers
title: Former Nunavut RCMP officer charged with sex assault
content:
Updated on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at 3 p.m. ET




A former Kinngait RCMP officer faces two counts of sexual assault for incidents alleged to have occurred while he was posted to the community’s detachment.




The Nunavut RCMP announced the charges against Edward George Zacher Tuesday in a news release. Later that day, RCMP released an update saying Calgary police laid the charges, but did not say when that happened.




Zacher is described in the news release as a “former” Nunavut RCMP officer. RCMP declined to say whether the 49-year-old remains a member of the force outside the territory.




The charges stem from incidents alleged to have occurred in 2023. The news release does not say when or where Zacher was arrested, but that he has been released from custody.




Zacher’s first court appearance is scheduled for Jan. 18 in Iqaluit.




This article has been updated to include information that police in Calgary laid the charges against Edward George Zacher.

title: ‘There’s probably 10,000 reasons’: MLA Brian Koonoo resigns from cabinet
content:
This story was updated Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at 6:05 p.m. ET.




Brian Koonoo has resigned as a Nunavut cabinet minister effective immediately, Premier John Main announced Monday evening, citing “personal reasons.”




In an interview, Koonoo said “there’s probably 10,000 reasons” for his decision.




“The main parts are my family’s homesick and we want to be together again,” he said. “And I would like to start supporting my constituency more in a full capacity, and also I miss hunting.”




Koonoo previously held three portfolios, including environment, energy, languages, and culture and heritage.




Cecile Nelvana Lyall, the minister responsible for the Nunavut Housing Corp., will take on environment and energy.




The languages and culture and heritage posts will go to Human Resources Minister Annie Tattuinee, who is also the minister responsible for the Workers’ Safety and Compensation Commission.
















This is Koonoo’s first term in the legislative assembly after being elected in the 2025 territorial election. He represents the Tununiq riding that consists of Pond Inlet. Koonoo a hunter, and children’s book author and former Parks Canada employee.




Koonoo was not present for Monday’s sitting of the legislative assembly.

author: Daron Letts
title: Cabinet to discuss Kitikmeot Inuit employment pilot project
content:
Nunavut’s cabinet ministers will discuss a proposed pilot project that would see only Inuit hired for territorial government positions in the Kitikmeot Region.




Human Resources Minister Annie Tattuinee says she will bring a proposal for a Kitikmeot-based Inuit hiring pilot project to cabinet. (Photo by Daron Letts)




Cambridge Bay MLA Fred Pedersen pitched the idea in the legislative assembly Monday.




“We can take it into consideration,” said Human Resources Minister Annie Tattuinee.




Pedersen’s proposal would see non-Inuit employees offered similar positions in 

other regions. Only Inuit would be allowed to replace them.




This practice would apply to positions that become open as non-Inuit staff retire. 

Pedersen suggested the pilot project could run for five years, but its length would be up to cabinet.




“I look forward to hearing what cabinet’s thoughts are on it,” he said during an interview.
















The current Inuit employment rate in the Kitikmeot is 57 per cent, slightly above the territorial average of approximately 50 per cent.




According to Article 23 of the Nunavut agreement, the government is obligated to pursue an 85-per-cent Inuit workforce. Eligible Inuit are defined as those enrolled as beneficiaries under Article 35 of the agreement.

title: PWHL team leads hockey camp for female players in Iqaluit
content:
Forty-seven girls in Iqaluit trained with a professional women’s hockey team over the weekend.




From right, players Sophia Mearns, Mary Suvega, Olivia Sulurayok and Hazel Kilukishak, in the back, await their turn to get back onto the ice between drills at a Nunavut Ukpiit Hockey Association camp. (Photo by Lilli Akpaleeapik)




The Nunavut Ukpiit Hockey Association hosted the camp Friday to Sunday at the Arctic Winter Games Arena in collaboration with the Toronto Sceptres, a Professional Women’s Hockey League team.




Professional players Emma Woods, Raygan Kirk and Brooke Disher arrived in Iqaluit Friday with Kate Germain, their strength and conditioning coach, to lead the event.




This was Woods’ second time visiting the territory for a hockey camp.




“It’s just been great to work with all the girls,” said Woods, a forward for the Sceptres. 




“You can just see they pay attention to everything we say, and you can see they’re learning throughout the weekend. Honestly it’s been such a treat coming up and working with this group.”
















The players and coach led workouts at Aqsarniit Middle School, on-ice drills and scrimmages.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Missing 14-year-old found safe, Ottawa police say
content:
A 14-year-old girl who was reported missing in Ottawa in the 1000 block of Gladstone Avenue last week has been found “safe and sound,” police say.




The Ottawa Police Service issued a release on Oct. 29 saying that the youth went missing the evening prior.




Police spokesperson Julie Kavanagh

ᒥ ᓵᓚᒃᓴᐅᓯᐊᕋᓱᒃᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᓄᓇᑦᓯᐊᕐᒥ, ᖃᐅᔨᒪᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᙱᑦᑐᖅ ᑖᓐᓇ ᓂᓪᓕᐊᑎᑕᐅᓂᐊᕆᐊᒃᓴᖓᓂ ᐱᙳᐊᕈᑎᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥᒃ ᐱᐅᓯᕚᓪᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓇᓱᒃᑐᒥ ᐃᓱᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᓄᐃᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᖏᓐᓂ.




ᐅᕙᓂ 

ᑕᕐᕆᔭᒐᖅ ᖃᒡᒋᖅᒥ,

 ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᖅᐹᖑᓂᖓᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᖓᓂ ᑕᕐᕆᔭᒐᖅ ᐱᙳᐊᕈᑎ ᐅᖄᓚᐅᑎᕋᓛᓄᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓂᐊᖅᖢᓂ, ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑐᑦ ᐃᙱᕐᑐᒥ ᑐᓴᕐᓴᐅᔪᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂ ᑕᕐᕆᔭᒐᕐᓂ ᓴᖅᑭᔮᖅᑎᑦᑎᓕᕌᖓᑕ.




“ᐃᙱᐅᑎᐅᑉ ᑎᑎᕋᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᖏᑦ ᐃᒪᓐᓇᐸᓘᕐᑐᑦ, ‘ᐊᖑᑎ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᑦᑎᐊᖅᑐᐊᓗᒃ ᐅᕙᓐᓄᑦ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᓱᓕ ᒪᒃᑯᒃᑐᑎᑦ. ᐃᓅᓯᖃᕈᑎᖃᐅᖅᖢᑎᑦ. ᓄᓇᕐᔪᐊᕐᓗ ᑕᑯᐊᓂᒃᓯᒪᙱᖢᒍᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᓪᓗᒃ, ᐃᒃᐱᐊᕐᔪᒃᒥᐅᑕᖅ, ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




“ᐅᓇ ᐱᐅᔪᐊᓗᒃ [ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓄᑦ] ᑐᓵᑎᖢᒋᑦ ᐃᖏᐅᑎᓂ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖏᑦᑎᒎᖓᔪᓂ. ᐅᕙᓐᓄᓪᓕ ᐃᓗᐊᕈᑎᒻᒪᕆᒐ ᐃᙱᕐᑎᐅᓪᓗᖓ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᖃᕈᓐᓇᕋᒪ ᑖᔅᓱᒧᖓ.”




ᔪᐊᒃ ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᐊᓗᒃᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓇᓱᒃᑎᐅᔪᑦ, ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᕐᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᔨᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᕙᓪᓕᐊᓕᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐱᙳᐊᕈᑎᒥ 2022-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᐅᓇ ᒪᓕᒃᑐᖅ ᐊᓛᓱᐊᒥ, ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᐊᑕᐅᔪᖅ, 7-ᓂ ᐊᔾᔨᒌᙱᑦᑑᑎᓂ ᐊᓂᒍᐃᕙᓪᓕᐊᓇᓱᒃᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓴᓇᔭᐅᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᖓᒍᑦ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓱᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᓄᐃᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᓴᓂᒃ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒧᑦ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨ ᔪᒌᑕ ᓯᖕ.
















ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᒥ ᓂᕐᔪᑎᙳᐊᖅ ᐃᒥᖅᑎᑦᑎᓇᓱᒃᖢᓂ ᐱᐅᙱᑦᑐᕈᓗᒥ ᐊᓛᓱᐊᒥ ᑲᑎᕐᓱᐃᓂᕐᒥᓂ ᐃᒪᑦᑎᐊᕙᒃᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓂᓚᖕᓂ. ᐱᙳᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕈᓐᓇᖅᑐᑦ ᑖᔅᓱᒥᖓ ᐱᑦᑕᐃᓕᒪᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓱᒫᓘᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᐊᓂᒍᖅᑎᑕᐅᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐃᒥᐊᓗᙱᒃᑲᓗᐊᕐᓗᑎ, ᓯᖕ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᓂᐱᓕᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᒥᔪᖅ ᐃᙱᑦᒥ ᑭᖓᕐᓂᑦ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᓘᓚ ᐅᓱᐃᑦᑐᒃ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᕿᓚᐅᔾᔭᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑭᒻᒥᕈᒻᒥᐅᑕᖅ ᓕᐅ ᑎᒥᓚ, ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᑲᑕᔾᔭᖅᑐᓂᒃ ᔭᓗᓇᐃᒥᐅᑖᖕᓂ ᑎᕕᓂ ᑯᓕᒃᑖᓇ ᐊᔭᓕᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑲᐃᓕ ᐃᓄᒃᓱᒃ ᒪᒦ, ᖃᐅᔨᒪᔭᐅᖕᒥᔪᖅ ᐱᖅᓯᖅᒥ.




ᐱᙳᐊᖅ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐅᕙᙵᑦ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 2025-ᒥ ᒪᐅᖓ ᔪᓚᐃ 2026-ᒧ, 276 ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂᙶᖅᑐᑦ 21-ᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒥ

title: Microplastics in lakes near Iqaluit likely come from local source: Study
content:
Microplastics that are present in lakes around Iqaluit likely come from a local source, according to findings from a recent study published in the journal Arctic Science.




Researchers sampled 19 lakes in 2022 and 2023, including nine east of Iqaluit and 10 north of the city. The highest concentration of particles was found in lakes east — or downwind — of Iqaluit.




Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic that have broken off from larger items, such as left-behind litter. They are known to be harmful to ecosystems and human health.




The direction the wind blows is important to take into consideration because microplastics can travel long distances by air, said Patricia Corcoran, a Western University professor in the earth sciences department, and one of authors of the study, “Microplastics in stair-step moss and lake water on Baffin Island, Nunavut, reflect a local source component.”




“Wherever we go, we’re shedding microplastics,” Corcoran said in an interview, speaking from London, Ont.




Microplastics can also make their way into lakes through tributaries, creeks and rivers. Human activity, such as boating and fishing, is also a factor, she said.




Researchers found the microplastics after collecting samples of moss, lake water and shoreline sediment. They discovered the particles were mainly concentrated in moss and lake water.

title: Professional women hockey players to lead training camp in Iqaluit
content:
A team of professional women hockey players is coming to Iqaluit this weekend to lead a hockey camp for girls.




The Nunavut Ukpiit Hockey Association has brought in three players from the Toronto Sceptres, who compete in the Professional Women’s Hockey League, to take part in strength and conditioning courses led by Sceptres training coach Kate Germain, according to an update on the association’s Facebook page.




Events are scheduled to start Friday at 4:30 p.m. and continue through Sunday. Girls registered with the Iqaluit Amateur Hockey Association are invited to take part.




Regularly scheduled events hosted at Arctic Winter Games Arena, such as public skating and other practices, have been cancelled to allow for the hockey camp programming.




According to the association’s website, the goal of this camp is to empower women’s hockey players across the territory, both in hockey and in life.

title: Kuujjuaq Greenhouse gets $1M in federal funding
content:
The Kuujjuaq Greenhouse has $1 million in federal funding to expand local food production and processing in the community.




Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty toured the greenhouse Friday morning as part of a funding announcement from Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions. It’s a federal program that gives financial support to small and medium-size businesses and non-profit organizations.




The money will go toward the construction of a new service building connected to the existing greenhouses that were built in 1999 and 2012, said Roxane Archambault, a member of the four-person volunteer committee managing the Kuujjuaq Greenhouse. The project is operated by the municipality.




The new building will include an insulated space to help extend the gardening season, washrooms and improved facilities to provide more comfortable working conditions, Archambault said. The committee also hopes to integrate a seedling container into the new building.




It will also support the greenhouse’s food-processing activities, preservation equipment and workshops on growing fresh food.

content:

title: Ottawa police ask residents to check sheds, garages in search for missing Inuk teen
content:
Ottawa police are asking residents in the 1000 block of Gladstone Avenue to check their properties and surveillance cameras as they continue searching for a missing 14-year-old girl.




Lydia Oyukuluk was last seen Wednesday, Oct. 28, at about 6 p.m. in the area, police said in a news release Thursday.







On Friday, police asked people in the area, including along Spadina Avenue and surrounding streets, to check backyards, sheds, garages and other places where Oyukuluk might have sought shelter.




They are also asking residents to review doorbell camera and surveillance footage from Wednesday evening onward for possible sightings.




Temperatures in Ottawa dropped to 8 C early Friday morning, according to Environment Canada online weather reports.




OPS media spokesperson 

Julie

 Kavanagh confirmed Friday that Oyukuluk is Inuk.




She is described as four-foot-nine with a petite build and long black hair partially dyed red at the back.



















She was last seen wearing baggy black sweatpants, a black camouflage hoodie and socks. She was not wearing shoes.




Anyone who sees Oyukuluk is asked to call 911 so she can receive immediate assistance, an updated release said. Anyone with information about her whereabouts can contact Ottawa police at 613-236-1222.

title: NuBrew stops canning, blames regulatory changes
content:
Nunavut Brewing Co., the sole local brewer in the territory, has stopped canning its beer after the territorial liquor commission made changes to the way it prices alcohol.




The markup applied by the Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission to NuBrew beer used to be 76 per cent less than what’s applied to beer imported into the territory. As of June 1, that difference was reduced to 40 per cent less.




“The difference between our markup and the big brewers like Anheuser-Busch has shrunk,” said Jordan Kennedy, interim manager of Nunavut Brewing Co.




“T

hose big brewers do not provide anything to this territory.

 They don’t pay payroll taxes. They don’t pay property taxes. 

They don’t employ people. They don’t contribute to the local economy like we do.”




Kennedy said he first learned of the the cost increase when a customer complained about an approximately $120 price hike to a keg of the company’s beer purchased through Iqaluit’s beer and wine store in late July.




Kennedy said when contacted the commission at the end of the summer, the response was a suggestion the brewery reduce the alcohol content in its products.

ᐃᓱᒪᑐᓂᕐᒥ, ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ 2026−ᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕐᔪᐊᖓᓂ ᓵᓚᖃᐅᓯᐊᖑᔪᒥ ᑐᓂᔭᐅᔪᓂ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 5−ᒥ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᒥ, ᐊᑦᑎᖅᓯᔪᒥ ᐊᕆᓐᓯᒥ ᐱᓂᖓᓂ ᓵᓚᖃᐅᓯᐊᒥᒃ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᐅᓂᖅᐹᖑᔪᒥ.




“ᐃᒃᐱᒍᓱᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᐅᕗᖅ ᐅᕙᓐᓄᑐᐊᖑᙱᑦᑐᖅ, ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᐃᒃᐱᒍᓱᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᐅᒋᕗᖅ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᒥᓱᓄᑦ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒋᔭᓐᓂ ᔮᓐ ᐊᕐᓇᓗᒃᔪᐊᖅ ᖁᑦᑎᒃᑐᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒥ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ. “ᐃᒃᐱᒍᓱᖕᓂᐅᕗᖅ, ‘ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᓪᓚᕆᐅᔪᒍᑦ. ᐱᓕᕆᓂᖃᓪᓚᕆᒃᐸᒃᐳᒍᑦ ᐅᕙᓂ.’”




ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᑳᕋᓂ ᐊᕐᕕᐊᓂᑦ, ᐊᕆᓐᓯ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᕙᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᓴᔅᑳᑦᓱᐊᓐᒥ. ᓅᕋᑖᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒧᑦ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᔾᔨᕈᓱᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑐᕌᒐᕆᔭᖓ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐱᐅᓂᖅᓴᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒻᒥᐅᓂ. ᑕᐃᒫᒃ ᑕᐅᑐᒃᑕᑐᐊᖃᑲᐃᓐᓇᓕᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐱᕈᖅᓴᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᒥᑦ.




“ᐱᕈᖅᓴᐃᑎᓪᓗᖓ ᐅᑯᓇᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᑖᒃᑯᓂᖓ, ᐅᒃᐱᕈᓱᖕᓂᖅᓴᐅᓕᖅᐳᑦ ᐅᕙᓐᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᒥᓱᓂ ᑐᓂᓯᕗᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᕈᑎᒃᓴᓂ ᖃᓄᖅ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᖓᓐᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᓕᓴᐃᓂᓐᓂᑦ,” ᐊᕆᓐᓯ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖓ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᖃᓐᓇᕆᔭᖓ ᐹᑎ ᔮᓐᔅᑕᓐ, ᐃᓕᓴᐃᔨᒻᒪᕆᖕᓄᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎ ᐊᒻᒪ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᐅᓂᖅᐹᖑᔪᒥ ᐃᒃᓯᕙᐅᑕᖓ ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᒡᔪᐊᒥ ᑭᐊᔾᒍᕆᒥ, ᓂᕈᐊᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐊᕆᓐᓯᒥ ᓵᓚᖃᐅᓯᐊᒃᓴᒧᑦ.

title: No charges against police involved in fatal 2025 Kangiqsualujjuaq shooting
content:
Quebec’s Director of Criminal and Pénal Prosecutions will not lay charges against a Nunavik Police Service officer who fatally shot a man in Kangiqsualujjuaq in May 2025, finding that the officer was justified in his use of lethal force under the Criminal Code.




The decision follows a review of the investigation conducted by the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes, according to a release issued by Quebec’s prosecutor’s office Wednesday.




The Nunavik Police Service had been searching for the Mark Annanack since April 5, 2025, after he escaped from custody at the Kangiqsualujjuaq police station.




On May 6, at around 10:25 p.m., officers found him hiding in a tent in a wooded area behind a house. When they approached him, he repeatedly claimed to have a knife and a firearm and threatened to use them, the release said.




Officers tried to persuade him to cooperate. When he attempted to leave the tent, police sprayed him in the face with pepper spray.




At around 10:39 p.m., the man exited the tent again and walked toward an officer. After being told the man had a knife, the officer ordered him to stop and fired two rounds from a Taser, according to the report.




The man remained standing and continued walking toward the officer, who then fired two gun shots.
















Annanack, was taken to a health centre, where he was pronounced dead at 11:47 p.m.

title: Ottawa police seek public’s help finding 14-year-old girl
content:
This story was updated on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at 10 a.m. ET because the missing teen has been found.




Ottawa police are asking the public to be on the lookout for a 14-year-old girl who has been reported missing in the city.




The girl was last seen at 6 p.m. on Wednesday in the 1000 block of Gladstone Avenue, according to a release Thursday from the Ottawa Police Service.




She was last seen wearing baggy black sweatpants, a black camouflage hoodie and socks of an unknown colour. She was not wearing shoes, the release said.




Police described her as Indigenous, four-foot-nine, with a petite build. She has long black hair that is partially dyed red at the back.




The police asked anyone with information on her whereabouts to call 613-236-1222, extension 2355.

title: Nunavimmiut Futures Fair completes 3-year tour of Nunavik
content:
The Nunavimmiut Futures Fair has completed a three-year tour of Nunavik, bringing employers, educational institutions and other organizations into high schools across the region to introduce students to potential career paths.




This edition of the fair wrapped up in Kuujjuaq on Oct. 27 and 28 at Jaanimmarik School after visiting Puvirnituq, Inukjuak, Quaqtaq and Tasiujaq.




More than 10 organizations were on hand to give presentations to high school students. Evening sessions were also held in the school gym Oct. 28.




Participants included the FCNQ Co-op, Kativik Regional Government, Air Inuit, the Canadian Coast Guard, Ungava Tulattavik Health Center, Sanajiit, Kativik Ilisarniliriniq and Pijunnaqunga.




The goal of this initiative is to introduce the work of different organizations and the opportunities available to them, said Joëlle Fares, project development officer in adult education and vocational training.




“This will guide them in terms of what they can be in the future,” she said.

launched

 in 2016, for three years. She said students often become more engaged as they attend presentations and learn about the different opportunities available to them.

title: Qajuqturvik hopes to start country food festival with a ‘bang,’ says centre’s leader
content:
The Qajuqturvik Community Food Centre in Iqaluit is preparing to roll out its first ever Country Food Festival.




The first of six meals offered during the weeklong event will be served Sunday, with two seatings of 60 people. Laakkuluk Williamson will curate and prepare the opening-day menu, which will feature inuksiut, or traditional food, from Nunavut and Kalaallit Nunaat, or Greenland.




On Monday, Laakkuluk Williamson will serve a variety of inuksiut from Kalaallit Nunaat, or Greenland, including smoked Maktaaq and dried fish. (Photo by Lilli Akpaleeapik)




The menu was inspired by Williamson’s continuous travel back and forth between her two homelands, Greenland and Nunavut.




“I’m very passionate about making sure that country food is part of our everyday experience as Inuit,” she said Wednesday in an interview at the food centre. “It’s wonderful to be able to show solidarity, that we have one culture, one language, through the food that we are having.”




Sunday’s plates will be filled with pitsi, or dried fish; maktaaq; uujuq, or stewed meat; and roasted tukuminiq, or caribou meat with gravy. To top it off will be a dessert of baked goods, applesauce and whipping cream topped with paurngait, or crow berries, and aqpiit, or cloudberries.

title: Kuujjuaq’s former elders’ home to undergo repairs before shelter opens
content:
Kuujjuaq’s former Tusaajiapik elders’ home will undergo repairs so it can safely accommodate the community’s homeless population, but it still won’t meet the standards required for a long-term care home, Nunavik health officials say.




Before the building opens as a temporary shelter, valves in its heating system will be replaced, the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services said in an email that communications co-ordinator Yentl Béliard-Joseph sent to Nunatsiaq News on Tuesday.




To do so, the heating system will need to be shut off for five days.




In April, the health board and Ungava Tulattavik Health Center cited problems with the building’s heating system and other “major technical components.” As a result, the organizations relocated residents to Montreal and closed the home.




On Friday, Deputy Mayor Claude Gadbois told Nunatsiaq News an agreement between the municipality, housing bureau, health board and health centre will allow the building to be used as a homeless shelter until October 2027.




He also said the building does not have a functioning sprinkler system.




Following a 2014 fire at a seniors’ home in L’Isle-Verte that killed 32 people, Quebec introduced requirements for automatic sprinkler systems in seniors’ residences housing 10 or more people. The deadline for facilities to comply was extended to December 2027.

title: Safety a concern in Pangnirtung after increase in RCMP calls: MLA
content:
Pangnirtung MLA Johnny Mike is calling for the territorial government to help stop alcohol and drugs from entering his community after calls to Pangnirtung RCMP went up in August.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: NTI commits $40.8M in federal funding toward health initiatives
content:
Over the next five years, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. is committing $40.8 million in federal funding to support health and wellness programs.




The organization made the announcement Oct. 21 in a news release.




The funding covers April 1, 2027 to March 31, 2032, and is intended to close the “gap in health outcomes between Inuit and other Canadians,” according to the release.




Nunatsiaq News has requested a copy of the full five-year spending plan from NTI but has not received a response.




In Iqaluit, the Umingmak child and youth advocacy centre and the Piruqatigiit Resource Centre, which provides support to those with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders and other conditions, are among those that will receive an unspecified amount of money.




As well, an unspecified portion of money is earmarked for Qaujigiartiit Health Research Centre’s Inunnguiniq childrearing and parenting training program, as well as its Makimautiksat Youth Camp, which aims to promote wellness by getting those aged nine to 12 out on the land.




NTI’s board of directors approved three other spending plans earlier this month aimed at strengthening Inuktut language training and advancing the elimination of tuberculosis.

content:
The Canadian Coast Guard is preparing to test the Arctic surveillance capacity of a large Israeli-manufactured drone.




Coast guard staff began testing the Hermes 900 Starliner earlier this year at the Canadian Forces Base in Greenwood, N.S., before it was disassembled and shipped from there to Iqaluit on Oct. 1.




The testing will part of an effort to study whether the drone can fit well into the coast guard’s fleet of smaller drones, said Mark McKeeman, the director of the coast guard’s remotely piloted aircraft program.




“Were still in the contract delivery stages with the manufacturer, so they have to prove that the aircraft is capable of operating in some of the conditions in the Arctic,” he said.




One of the things the Hermes 900 Starliner will be tested for is its ability to operate at 72 degrees north, which is about the same latitude as Pond Inlet.




Canada signed a contract to obtain the drone from the Israeli arms dealer Elbit Systems in 2020, at a cost of $36 million.




Transport Canada was initially assigned to manage its use as part of Canada’s National Aerial Surveillance Program, which was transferred over to the coast guard on April 1.

title: Horror writer Jamesie Fournier shares scares in print and on screen
content:
Horror author Jamesie Fournier says he enjoys scaring children almost as much as they enjoy being scared.




“It’s very entertaining to be terrified,” he said Saturday in an interview in his Inhabit Media office in Iqaluit. “That’s why we love horror.”




The Inuktitut and English writer had just launched his latest children’s book,

 Lemming’s First Halloween

, earlier that day at Nunatta Sunakkutaangit Museum.




Dozens of costumed children and their families dropped by the event to create creepy crafts and hear spooky stories.




The book is Fournier’s second in the series. He published 

Lemming’s First Christmas

 in English and Inuktitut in 2024. 

Lemming’s First Halloween 

marks Fournier’s first collaboration with Toronto-based Pakistani-Canadian illustrator Faiza Khan.




The tale follows Lemming and her pup as they cross paths with a qallupilluk, a monster known to drag children into the ocean.




Overcoming fear is an important life skill that Inuit horror stories tap into, Fournier said.
















“When you’re afraid you’re aware of your surroundings. You’re taking everything in. You’re being very cautious. Survivalism has kicked in,” he said. “To be brave we have to first know what scares us.”




Scary fiction help children remember life lessons that can help keep them safe, such as to stay away from sea ice when a trusted adult is not near.

ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᒃ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓃᑦᑐᖅ ᖁᑦᑎᒃᓯᓯᒪᓂᑯᒥ ᓄᓇᒥ ᒥᑦᑕᕐᕕᐅᑉ ᖃᓂᒋᔭᖓᓂ.




ᖃᓄᐃᓕᖓᓂᖓ ᓄᓇ ᑕᐅᑐᒃᖢᒍ ᓲᕐᓗ ᐊᔾᔨᖃᖅᑰᔨᔪᖅ ᐊᑎᖓᓂ — ᐸᖕᓂᖅ, ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑐᑦ ᐊᖑᓴᓪᓗᒃ ᑐᒃᑐ ᐸᖕᓂᖅ. ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᑐᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᓚᐅᕐᑐᑦ ᐊᑎᖓᓂ ᓂᕈᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐊᕐᕌᓂ ᓵᓚᒃᓴᕋᓱᒃᖢᑎᒃ ᐊᑎᒃᓴᖓᓂ.




“ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᒃ ᐱᐅᔪᐊᓗᒃ — ᓴᓇᓯᒪᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᓂ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᓕᓴᐃᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᔭᐅᓕᕐᑐᖅ ᕌᑦᓂ ᑐᕉᕗ ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 14-ᒥ ᐅᖄᓚᐅᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ.




ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᒃᒧᑦ 16 ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖏᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ 200 ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᑎᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᕐᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒍᕇᑦ 7-ᒥ 12-ᒧ ᐅᑭᐅᒃᓵᖅ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᓕᕆᐊᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐊᖏᓂᖃᖅᑐᒥᓐ 3,300 ᑭᑉᐹᕆᒃᑎᓯᒪᔪᓂ ᒦᑕᓂ ᑕᐃᒪᙵᑦ ᓴᓇᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐱᐊᓂᒃᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐱᐊᓂᒃᑕᐅᕝᕕᒃᓴᖓᓂ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑕᐅᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ 2023-ᒥ.




ᐅᓇ ᑕᓪᓕᒪᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᓂ ᓴᓇᔭᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᐅᕙᒃᑐᒥ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᐱᓕᑕᒃ ᐊᓐᑐᐳᕋᐃᔅ ᓕᒥᑎᑦᑯᓐᓂ, ᐅᐃᓂᐱᒡᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓕᖕᓂ ᐋᑭᐅᑕᒃᑯᓐᓂᑦ (Accutech Engineering Inc.), ᐊᒻᒪ ᐹᑭᓐ ᐃᒡᓗᒃᓴᓂ ᑎᑎᕋᐅᔭᖅᑎᓂᒃ ᑖᒃᑯᐊᓗ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᕕᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᐋᓐᑎᐅᕆᐅᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐳᕆᑎᔅ ᑲᓚᒻᐱᐊᒥ.
















ᐅᓇ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᒃ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᒃᑰᖓᔪᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᓇᖅᑐᑦ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᐃᓚᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᕿᔪᓕᐅᕈᑎᓂ, ᑐᓴᕐᓴᐅᔾᔪᑎᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᑎᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑕᕐᕆᔭᕈᓐᓇᐅᑎᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᑕᒪᕐᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕕᐅᔪᑦ, ᑐᕉᕗ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




“ᑭᓱᖃᑦᑎᐊᐸᓗᒃᑐᖅ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, ᐅᖃᒃᑲᓐᓂᖅᖢᓂ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑐᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃ “ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᐊᓗᒃᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕕᐅᓇᔭᕐᒥᔪᖅ.”




ᓂᕿᓕᐅᕐᕕᒥ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕐᓴᕐᕕᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕐᕕᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᒪᑯᐊ ᐃᓐᓇᑐᖃᐃᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᔾᔪᑎᒋᔪᓐᓇᖅᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᓲᕐᓗ ᐋᒃᑐᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓂᕿᓕᕆᕝᕕᖓᓂ ᐱᑕᖃᖅᖢᓂ.




ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᓕᓵᐸᓗᒃᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᑏᑦ. ᐊᑐᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᓄᑖᓂ ᐃᒐᓂ ᐅᒥᖕᒪᓕᐅᖅᖢᑎᒃ. ᐅᒃᑑᐱᕆ 14-ᒥ ᓇᑦᑎᓕᐅᑲᑕᓚᐅᕆᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᑖᓐᓇ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᒃ ᒪᑐᐃᖅᑕᐅᒻᒪᕆᒃᐸᑦ ᓂᕆᔭᐅᓂᐊᕐᑐᓂ.

title: Jimmy Bell – An Arctic trader
content:
Young Jimmy Bell stood 5’10” tall and weighed about 170 pounds when he joined the Hudson’s Bay Co. as a 19-year-old recruit in 1925. 




Two decades later his weight had more than doubled, by some reports reaching 350 pounds. The Inuit, whom he knew and loved, and who knew and loved him, called him Quinijuq – the fat man.




Bell was born in Cromdale, Scotland, the eldest son in a large family. He walked three miles to school and back each day during eight years of primary school and followed that with three years of higher education. 




Then Bell worked as a bookkeeper for a local garage for three years until he emigrated to Canada as a young fur trader, following in the footsteps of so many young Scots before him. 




Montreal, the city where he first set foot in Canada, was always dear to him. Much later, he decided that he would eventually retire there, but it was never to be.




That summer of 1925 he travelled on the Hudson’s Bay Company supply ship to Lake Harbour (now Kimmirut) where he was apprentice clerk for three years, before moving on to Frobisher Bay for two years in the same position. 




After a year’s furlough, Bell was posted for one year as manager at Payne Bay in northern Quebec, a post he described as the poorest-looking he had seen. He followed that with two years each again in Frobisher Bay and Lake Harbour.

title: Housing, homelessness in focus in Ottawa’s Rideau-Vanier race
content:
Six candidates are vying to represent Ottawa’s Rideau-Vanier ward ahead of next week’s municipal election, with housing, homelessness and support for the Inuit community among campaign issues.




Ottawans are set to elect ward councillors Monday to a four-year term. Rideau-Vanier includes Vanier, sometimes called “Little Nunavut,” home to an urban Inuit community.




Statistics Canada counted 1,270 Inuit in Ottawa in the 2021 census.




Lyra Evans, Julie Fiala Chartrand, Brian Paquette and Michael Karl Sewanaku spoke with Nunatsiaq News about issues that could impact Inuit residents in the ward.




Evans, a former Ottawa-Carleton District School Board trustee and chair, said residents have raised concerns about homelessness, addiction, poverty and food insecurity.




“Pushing people out of a park and destroying all their belongings doesn’t stop them from being homeless,” Evans said, criticizing the city’s approach to encampments.
